args: Existing research, open-source projects, datasets, and commercial products for tracing a song melody snippet back to its earliest/original source ("melodic ancestry" or provenance tracing) — e.g. the "dance the night away" hook in J.Lo's "On the Floor" deriving from Los Kjarkas' "Llorando se fue" (via Kaoma's "Lambada"). Cover: (1) academic MIR research on cross-version / cover song identification, melodic similarity, query-by-humming, symbolic melody retrieval, plagiarism/musical-borrowing detection, and folk-tune variant/tune-family clustering (e.g. Meertens Tune Collections, Dutch Song Database, Peachnote, Themefinder, Musipedia, SIMSSA, "The Musical Plagiarism" datasets); (2) systems that build derivation GRAPHS rather than pairwise matches — sample/cover/interpolation knowledge bases (WhoSampled, SecondHandSongs, MusicBrainz work relationships, Discogs, Wikidata), phylogenetic / stemmatic methods applied to music, and any work on inferring directionality/ancestry (who copied whom) rather than mere similarity; (3) commercial products: music plagiarism detection and rights-clearance tools (Musical AI, Sureel, Pex, Audible Magic, ACRCloud, Sound Sample Detection / Rightsify, Deezer/Spotify internal work, Adrian Wong / Rightsify, Matchtune), song-ID apps (Shazam, SoundHound, Aha Music) and their limits on melody-only matching; (4) the technical building blocks an ML pipeline would use in 2025-2026: automatic music transcription (basic-pitch, MT3, Omnisia), predominant melody extraction (melodia, CREPE), audio embeddings for cover detection (CQT-Net, ByteCover, Re-MOVE, DiscogsEffnet/CLMR/MERT), symbolic melody n-gram indexing, alignment/edit-distance under transposition and rhythm changes, plus vector search at catalog scale; benchmark datasets (Da-TACOS, SHS100K, Covers80, DALI, MTG-Jamendo) and reported accuracy numbers; (5) known hard problems and legal/musicological caveats: public-domain/folk melodies with no single originator, oral-tradition transmission, contrafacta, false positives from common melodic archetypes, expert-witness forensic musicology practice, and what courts/datasets treat as "substantial similarity". Prioritize concrete named systems, papers with results, repos, APIs, and datasets a builder could actually use, plus honest assessment of what does NOT exist yet.

phases.title: Scope
phases.detail: Decompose question (from args) into 5 search angles

phases.title: Search
phases.detail: 5 parallel WebSearch agents, one per angle

phases.title: Fetch
phases.detail: URL-dedup, fetch top 15 sources, extract falsifiable claims

phases.title: Verify
phases.detail: 3-vote adversarial verification per claim (need 2/3 refutes to kill)

phases.title: Synthesize
phases.detail: Merge semantic dupes, rank by confidence, cite sources

result.summary: Across 22 independently verified claims, the picture is consistent: the pairwise half of "melodic ancestry" is a solved-enough engineering problem, and the ancestry half is not. Catalog-scale version retrieval works — ByteCover-style fixed-length audio embeddings (ResNet-IBN50 + GeM + BNNeck) hit mAP 0.714 on Da-TACOS / 0.836 on SHS100K and reduce to 128–256-d vectors for ANN search, replacing DTW/Qmax time-series matching — and there are demonstrated symbolic pipelines (Needleman-Wunsch alignment over 10,062 folk melodies; BMM-Det bipartite max-matching over MIDI) plus a fully open-source phylogenetic toolchain (MAFFT to a chant-specific MrBayes fork to treeannotator to phyx) that actually builds derivation TREES rather than pairwise scores. But every verified system either infers similarity without direction, or gets direction handed to it: the one working multi-hop ancestry system (Bryan and Wang's Katz-centrality analysis, where tuning alpha visibly shifts credit for the "Amen" break from The Winstons toward Jester Hairston) runs on 42,447 human-curated WhoSampled records, not on audio; and where a method did try to infer direction, rooting failed and required manual musicological override. Generalization is the second hard wall: MelodySim scores 0.98 F1 on its own synthetic augmentations but 0.73 F1 (0.62 precision, mostly false positives) on real court cases — barely beating naive DTW-CQT at 0.72 and losing to it on accuracy — while BMM-Det drops to 0.33 top-1 when melodies are transformed by a VAE, and real ground-truth plagiarism data remains vanishingly small (29 pairs in 2021, ~70 by 2025). No verified evidence was found for any end-to-end audio-to-provenance-graph system, academic or commercial; a builder in 2026 would be assembling one from cover-ID embeddings, symbolic alignment, and a curated relationship graph, with directionality supplied by release-date metadata and human curation rather than learned.

findings.claim: Audio cover-song identification via fixed-length embeddings is the mature, catalog-scalable building block: ByteCover (ByteDance AI Lab + Peking University, ICASSP 2021) — ResNet-50 with IBN blocks, GeM pooling, BNNeck joint softmax+triplet training — reports Da-TACOS mAP 0.714 / P@10 0.801 / MR1 23.0, SHS100K-TEST 0.836 / 0.534 / 47.3, Covers80 0.906, Youtube350 0.955, beating CQT-Net (0.655 SHS100K), MOVE (0.507) and Re-MOVE (0.534) on Da-TACOS. Its 2048-d embeddings reduce to 256-d at mAP 0.653 and 128-d at 0.615, compared by cosine/Euclidean distance, which is what makes ANN vector search over a full catalog feasible instead of exhaustive DTW/Qmax matching.
findings.evidence: Three separate 3-0 verifications against the primary arXiv PDF, with Tables 1 and 2 extracted verbatim by pypdf: 'ByteCover 0.714 0.801 23.0' (Da-TACOS), 'ByteCover 0.836 0.534 47.3' (SHS100K), and '128 256 2048 ... mAP 0.615 0.653 0.714'. Architecture verbatim in the abstract: 'integration of instance normalization (IN) and batch normalization (BN) to build IBN blocks' and 'the BNNeck method to allow a multi-loss training ... jointly optimize a classification loss and a triplet loss'; ResNet-50 and GeM pooling confirmed in the body. The scalability rationale is the paper's own framing, not an interpolation: fixed-length vectors can be 'efficiently indexed and retrieved using existing nearest-neighbor search libraries, even for a large dataset', explicitly contrasted with DTW methods that 'contain exhaustive iteration and matching, which makes it difficult for them to scale'.

findings.claim: ByteCover's numbers are a 2021 baseline, not the 2026 ceiling, and its architecture is the reference template rather than current SOTA. ByteCover2 (ICASSP 2022) and ByteCover3 (ICASSP 2023) supersede the dimensionality-reduction figures (ByteCover2-128 outperforms ByteCover-2048), and CoverHunter (arXiv 2306.09025) reports a further ~17.7% gain on Da-TACOS, with 2024-2026 work shifting toward transformer/SSL backbones.
findings.evidence: Raised consistently as a currency qualification by verifiers of the ByteCover claims. The ACM survey 'Cover Song Identification Technologies: A Survey' confirms ByteCover2/3 reuse the ResNet-IBN50+BNNeck stack and that CoverHunter 'chose ResNet-IBN 50 as the backbone' following ByteCover — but CoverHunter itself reports +7.5% from replacing that backbone with a Conformer. Also a fair-comparison detail: 8,373 of Da-TACOS's 15,000 performances overlap SHS100K-TRAIN, so ByteCover's 0.714 comes from a retrained model, and the Re-MOVE comparison is not embedding-size-matched (ByteCover 256-d scores 0.653 vs Re-MOVE 256-d 0.524, a narrower gap than 0.714 vs 0.534 implies). Verified as secondary/corroborating context rather than as a first-class primary claim.

findings.claim: Melody-aware audio similarity for plagiarism has an open dataset, model and code — MelodySim (SUTD AMAAI Lab, arXiv 2505.20979): 1,568 Slakh2100 multi-track MIDI files augmented into 6,272 full-length audio files (each original plus three melody-preserving variations: note splitting, chord inversion/arpeggiation, instrument replacement, stem dropout, pitch/time/tempo shift), with a triplet network over a FROZEN MERT-v1-95M encoder (layers 3/6/9/12) plus a 1D convolutional ResNet and sigmoid classifier on 10-second segments; piece-level decisions come from thresholding a segment-by-segment similarity matrix and requiring a proportion of matches in both directions. Code at github.com/AMAAI-Lab/MelodySim, data at huggingface.co/datasets/amaai-lab/melodySim (CC-BY-3.0, 191,547 rows, 296 GB), weights at huggingface.co/amaai-lab/MelodySim.
findings.evidence: Two 3-0 verifications against the primary PDF plus live checks of the released artifacts. Paper section 4.2 verbatim: 'the proposed music similarity model is a triplet neural network (TNN) composed of a MERT encoder, a 1D ResNet backbone, and a classification head' and 'The MERT parameters remain frozen during training.' Section 4.3 gives the aggregation rule: 'when the proportional threshold is set to 0.2, then if more than 20% of segments in both directions exceed the similarity threshold, the pair is considered as too-similar.' One discrepancy a builder should know: the released GitHub/HF version states '1,710 valid synthesized pieces ... each containing 4 different versions ... total duration of 419 hours' (6,840 files) versus the paper's 1,568 pieces / 6,272 files. Authors themselves flag the piece-level aggregation as 'heuristic and may not generalize to diverse musical styles.'

findings.claim: Audio melody-similarity models do NOT transfer from synthetic training data to real infringement cases, and on real cases barely beat naive DTW. MelodySim scores 0.98 weighted song-level F1 on its own test split but only 0.73 F1 / 0.62 precision / 0.87 recall / 0.67 accuracy on MCIC (Music Copyright Infringement Cases, Park et al. 2024, 116 actual court cases), with 61 false positives vs 15 false negatives. On MCIC the baselines are DTW-CQT 0.72 F1 / 0.71 accuracy, DTW-chroma 0.69, DTW-pitch (pYIN) 0.68 — i.e. DTW-CQT beats the learned model on accuracy — even though in-domain the learned model crushes DTW (0.98 vs 0.79). A cleaner 2-fold-CV MelodySim row scores 0.70 F1, below DTW-CQT.
findings.evidence: Two 3-0 verifications, Table 3 and Table 4 extracted verbatim: 'MelodySim (overall) 101 61 55 15 0.62 0.87 0.73 0.67', 'DTW with CQT 94 51 65 22 0.65 0.81 0.72 0.71', 'MelodySim (2-fold CV) 103 77 39 13 0.57 0.89 0.70 0.61'. Authors' own framing is softer than 'collapses' ('generalize moderately'; the gap 'reflects the controlled nature of synthetic augmentations') but the arithmetic supports the harsher reading. Two methodological wrinkles strengthen rather than weaken the finding: the 0.73 row's aggregation threshold was tuned by cross-validation ON MCIC, and the MCIC split labels all 116 case pairs positive regardless of court outcome (66 of the cases were actually denied), so the ground truth is weaker than 'court-adjudicated' implies. Note also the v2 (Nov 2025) revision carries the MCIC evaluation; the May 2025 v1 does not.

findings.claim: Symbolic (MIDI) plagiarism detection has a released, peer-reviewed, fine-grained system: BMM-Det (ACM Multimedia 2023; arXiv 2107.09889) cuts two melodies into overlapping segment-level clips that become the two vertex sets of a bipartite graph — using relative pitch, relative duration and a downbeat indicator, with edges weighted by edit distance — and scores plagiarism as the optimal Kuhn-Munkres matching, returning colored, localized matched fragments rather than one global similarity number. Code and data at github.com/xuan301/BMMDet_MPDSet (MIT, live).
findings.evidence: 3-0 verification with every component checked against the arXiv HTML and the live repo (HTTP 200, MIT, Codes/Edit-Distance/, build_dataset/, data/). Abstract: 'a graph-based method called Bipatite Melody Matching Detector (BMM-Det), which formulates the problem as a max matching problem in the bipartite graph.' Fig. 3: 'The same color in the figure denotes the fine-grained plagiarized parts detected by BMM-Det.' Minor nit: the implementation minimizes total edit-distance cost, equivalent to maximizing similarity weight. A second mirror repo exists (github.com/hotelll/Music_Plagiarism_Detection) attached to the earlier version; both resolve.

findings.claim: BMM-Det degrades catastrophically exactly where a provenance system needs to work — on substantively transformed melodies. On MPD-Set, transposition is trivial (all methods 1.00 accuracy, average index 1.00) and BMM-Det handles pitch shift and duration variance at 0.98-1.00, but on 'Melody Change' fragments rewritten by the MuseMorphose Transformer-VAE its top-1 accuracy falls to 0.33 with average rank index 6.89 — still far above baselines (TF-IDF 0.08, Tversky 0.14, Sum Common 0.04, Ukkonen 0.06), but nowhere near usable. The authors note part of this may be irreducible: a VAE-rewritten melody 'despite being derived from the original song, may exhibit significant differences,' so the number conflates detector weakness with genuine loss of derivable signal.
findings.evidence: 3-0 verification with Table 3 extracted verbatim from arxiv.org/html/2107.09889: BMM-Det columns Transposition 1.00/1.00, Pitch Shifts 1.02/0.98, Duration Variance 1.00/1.00, Melody Change 6.89/0.33. This is the authors' own worst-case result against their own method — the opposite of a promotional benchmark. One imprecision in the original framing: 'every method reaches 1.00' is true for transposition only, not pitch shift (baselines 0.82-0.92). The paper also internally contradicts itself between prose and Table 3 on the Pitch Shifts vs Duration Variance columns. Nothing published since (MelodySim 2025; J. Audio Speech Music Proc. 2025) reports MPD-Set Melody Change results or claims to have solved VAE-transformed retrieval — MelodySim's augmentations deliberately PRESERVE melody, an easier regime.

findings.claim: Ground-truth plagiarism data is the binding constraint on the whole field, and it has barely grown in five years. BMM-Det's real-world evaluation set is 29 song pairs (20 legally adjudicated by courts via Cronin 2016, 9 from a Ping An Tech demo repo), all positives; the authors had to synthesize a 2,000-piece MPD-Set from Wikifonia MusicXML-to-MIDI because prior datasets (Mullensiefen and Pendzich 2009, Columbia Law School, MIREX) 'are not public and also out-of-date.' By 2025 the successor SMP dataset (Mippia, arXiv 2509.08282, github.com/Mippia/smp_dataset) offers only ~70 real-world pairs and self-describes as 'currently a sample-scale dataset designed to demonstrate our approach and methodology.'
findings.evidence: 3-0 verification; the outdatedness challenge was the strongest refutation avenue and it failed — real ground truth grew roughly 29 to ~70 pairs between 2021 and 2025. MelodySim independently notes plagiarism research 'remains challenging due to the absence of clearly defined plagiarism rules and datasets' and builds a synthetic set for the same reason. Independent search for a large public court-case benchmark surfaced nothing beyond the same ~20 US cases in the Cronin/Mullensiefen lineage. The MCIC set (116 cases) is the largest real-case resource that appeared anywhere in this corpus. Practical implication: any 2026 builder is training on synthetic augmentations and evaluating on ~100 real pairs.

findings.claim: Existing plagiarism/similarity systems output a SYMMETRIC magnitude and explicitly leave who-copied-whom to humans. BMM-Det's edit-distance costs are symmetric by construction (insertion cost = deletion cost = 1; substitution cost symmetric in its arguments) and the Kuhn-Munkres matching is invariant under swapping the two vertex sets, so no chronology or provenance signal enters the pipeline at any point; the authors position it as a transparent 'white-box' auxiliary tool with a user-chosen threshold, stating 'the determination of music plagiarism ultimately falls within the realm of legal judgment.' MelodySim likewise measures symmetric similarity only.
findings.evidence: 2-1 verification (dissent was on wording, not substance). Verbatim from the Conclusion: 'We have made efforts to design our method as a transparent white-box approach, but we acknowledge that the final determination of music plagiarism is ultimately a legal matter ... we envision our method as a valuable auxiliary tool.' Two wording corrections verifiers insisted on: (a) drop 'only a score' — BMM-Det's headline contribution IS segment-level localization, so it outputs a symmetric magnitude PLUS matched fragments, never a directional verdict; (b) soften 'explicitly does not adjudicate' to 'the method has no mechanism for' directionality — the paper never addresses direction, and its title ('Revealing Plagiarists') loosely implies a culprit it cannot identify.

findings.claim: Query-by-humming degrades sharply at catalog scale and remains behind commercial systems. On DB90K (90,000+ real song recordings), the best fused model trained on covers+hummings reaches only 0.776 top-100 / 0.707 top-10 / 0.586 top-3 on hummed queries, versus 0.899 top-10 on sung karaoke queries and versus 0.883-0.921 top-10 on small ~2,000-song academic benchmarks. On the MIREX QbH benchmarks the same academic deep model trails the ACRCloud proprietary system: 0.921 vs 0.990 (Jang), 0.966 vs 0.986 (Thinkit), 0.959 vs 0.972 (Subtask 2); crucially ACRCloud has no published numbers on the two real-audio sets (Jang Real 0.868, MTG-QBH 0.883), so the commercial-vs-academic gap is unmeasured precisely where provenance tracing on real recordings lives.
findings.evidence: Two verifications (2-1 and 3-0) against the ISMIR 2023 paper (Amatov et al., HSE Moscow / Huawei Noah's Ark Lab), Tables 1 and 2 extracted verbatim with pypdf. Important confounds the verifiers isolated: the humming-vs-singing gap is not purely modality — singing = 2,000 fragments from only 5 target songs vs humming = 126 fragments from 126 distinct songs, and n=126 gives ~+/-4% standard error on 0.707; and the small-benchmark-to-DB90K comparison mixes feature sets (CREPE+DTW in Table 1, CQT+Pearson reranking in Table 2), so like-for-like CQT is 0.747 to 0.595, a real but smaller drop than 0.921 to 0.707 implies. The ACRCloud/Stasiak rows are copied from the independently run MIREX 2016 leaderboard (IMIRSEL-evaluated, not vendor self-report), but are leaderboard-to-leaderboard, not a controlled head-to-head. 'Stasiak produced near-random results' refers to the authors' own reimplementation, not Stasiak's original system, which actually beat their model on two sets.

findings.claim: Cover-song data can substitute for scarce humming data in training melody-query systems, but only partially: the ISMIR 2023 authors treat QbH as 'a specialized case of cover song identification,' collect 308+ hours of additional time-aligned cover fragments via a semi-supervised loop that iteratively retrains the fingerprint encoder, and release CHAD (code at github.com/amanteur/CHAD, humming subset on HuggingFace) — but conclude that 'the pure search-by-humming setup requires adding a portion of real humming data into the training set for acceptable performance.'
findings.evidence: 3-0 verification, all five elements verbatim in the primary source. Backed by numbers, not just prose: on DB90K humming queries, covers-only training gives 0.759/0.621/0.603/0.517 (top-100/10/5/3) vs 0.776/0.707/0.691/0.586 with humming added, while on sung queries covers-only shows no drop (0.931 vs 0.923 top-100) — exactly the asymmetry claimed. Caveats: the 308 h cover corpus and DB90K are internal and unreleased; only the humming subset is public.

findings.claim: Bioinformatics sequence alignment is a demonstrated, published method for finding tune-family/variant relationships at ~10k-melody scale: Savage et al. (Current Biology 2022) encoded 10,062 Japanese and English/British-American folk melodies as strings over a 12-symbol scale-degree alphabet, aligned them with Needleman-Wunsch (gap-open 0.8, gap-extend 0.2), and recovered 328 pairs of highly related melodies at >=85% percent identity. The method lineage is explicit (Savage and Atkinson, 'Automatic Tune Family Identification by Musical Sequence Alignment,' ISMIR 2015).
findings.evidence: 3-0 verification; abstract confirmed verbatim via PubMed (cell.com and sciencedirect 403 automated fetch). Data and code released via the comp-music-lab GitHub organization. Four limitations that matter for a provenance product, all raised by the verifier and none refuting the claim: (a) automated alignments were of 'poor quality' and had to be manually corrected against original score notation, so pair DETECTION was automated corpus-wide but ALIGNMENT was not hands-off (critique from McBride and Fitch, arXiv 2607.12673); (b) all 328 related pairs are within-tradition (242 English-English, 86 Japanese-Japanese) — no highly related cross-cultural pairs were found, so this is not evidence the method bridges traditions the way a Llorando se fue to Lambada to On the Floor chain requires; (c) the paper estimates mutation rates and infers NO directionality; (d) input is symbolic notation, so an audio-first pipeline still needs transcription/melody-extraction front-ends this work does not supply.

findings.claim: Melodic evolution has measurable, non-uniform structure that should be encoded in the scoring function rather than using flat edit distance or default biological gap penalties: notes with stronger rhythmic function (final or stressed) are significantly more conserved than unstressed/ornamental notes, and substitutions concentrate between neighboring scale degrees — an empirical basis for a weighted substitution matrix and position-dependent scoring. Separately, insertions/deletions outnumber substitutions in sung folk-tune evolution, the opposite of genetic sequence evolution, meaning aligners must tolerate heavy ornamentation-driven length change.
findings.evidence: The substitution/conservation half verified 3-0 (verbatim: 'notes with stronger rhythmic functions are less likely to change' and 'note substitutions are most likely between neighboring notes'; four-level taxonomy final > stressed > unstressed > ornamental; holds independently in both corpora despite different tonal systems). Independently corroborated by prior MIR practice: van Kranenburg's Meertens Institute work on Dutch folk-song variants ('Musical Models for Melody Alignment,' ISMIR 2009) already uses metrical-accent weights in alignment for variant retrieval. The indel half verified only 2-1 and is representation-dependent: McBride and Fitch (arXiv 2607.12673, ~40,000 Irish dance tune variants) argue Savage's indel count conflates note SUBDIVISION/FUSION with true indels — 'our grid representation maps subdivided notes onto the metrical grid rather than onto gaps, they are absorbed as one-to-many correspondences and never counted as indels' — while conceding the distinction is genre-dependent and that in sung traditions (Savage's corpora) the same event IS a true indel. There is also mild circularity: the measured indel-to-substitution ratio is partly a function of the chosen 0.8/0.2 gap penalties. Both papers nonetheless agree default biological gap penalties should not be reused. Downgraded to medium for two reasons: the split vote, and the untested domain transfer — all evidence is oral-transmission folk tune families, not recording-mediated commercial pop hook borrowing, and neither paper reports retrieval-accuracy gains from weighted scoring.

findings.claim: A complete, open-source phylogenetic toolchain for building melodic derivation TREES already exists and is directly reusable: Genome of Melody (Hajic jr., Lanz, Ballen; Phil. Trans. R. Soc. B 380:20240274, 2025) encodes melodies as pitch sequences, aligns them with MAFFT v7.505, runs Bayesian phylogenetic inference in 'mrbayes volpiano' — a chant-specific fork of MrBayes v3.2.7a where 'standard character coding is no longer intended for morphology in biological datasets but rather for the encoding of plainchant melodies' — summarizes a maximum-clade-credibility tree with treeannotator, and formats with phyx. All code and data are released: github.com/Genome-of-Melody, github.com/gaballench/mrbayes_volpiano, Zenodo DOIs 10.5281/zenodo.13344525 and 10.5281/zenodo.14768498.
findings.evidence: 3-0 verification. Royal Society is paywalled (403, non-OA, PMID 41537896) but the author preprint (EcoEvoRxiv 8599) contains the quoted methods verbatim, and all five URLs return HTTP 200 with the Zenodo records resolving. The open-access companion paper (Ballen, Muhlova, Hajic jr., PLOS ONE, PMC13221024) independently corroborates the identical toolchain including the Mk model. Two qualifications: (a) tree tips are manuscript SOURCES (23 retained sigla) with melody variants of shared Cantus IDs as characters — this is stemmatics of variants of the same chant across witnesses, not a cross-song derivation graph linking distinct works; (b) input is monophonic, rhythm-free, volpiano-alphabet symbolic notation, so 'directly reusable' applies to the TOOLING, not the input representation — a pop-audio builder needs transcription and re-encoding layers first.

findings.claim: Inferring the ROOT — who came first, the direction of descent — is the demonstrated weak link, and in practice required manual musicological override. Gregorian chant has no usable outgroup (Old Roman chant is a candidate but its relationship is too unclear to use), so root position was estimated by Bayesian model selection via stepping stones; on the Introits dataset both top candidate roots (P~0.52 at branch 18, P~0.42) were judged historically implausible and the authors re-rooted by hand 'on the Rhine' at edge 4, stating the model selection method 'behaved in a faulty manner.'
findings.evidence: 3-0 verification; all three components verbatim in the primary text, including the authors' admission against interest. The published version independently returns 'the introits were manually rooted at edge 4 instead, keeping in mind that model selection on introits did not give good results.' Two caveats: rooting failed only on Introits — the Christmas dataset rooted automatically at model PP = 0.75 with a historically plausible west-/east-Frankish split — so this is a demonstrated failure on one of two datasets, not universal; and the paper flags a second weakness the claim omits ('even with the root selected musicologically, the clock model needs more'). The paper is also internally inconsistent about whether the P~0.42 root is branch 24 (body) or branch 16 (Fig. 5b caption), though both agree on the probabilities.

findings.claim: The only verified working multi-hop ancestry system gets its directionality handed to it by human curation, not inferred from audio: Bryan and Wang (ISMIR 2011, Stanford CCRMA) built their influence network entirely from a WhoSampled.com dataset of 42,447 user-generated sampling records — each a directed source-to-destination song-artist pair with release year, genre, collaborators, producers and part-sampled (vocals/drums/etc.), explicitly excluding cover-song entries — with zero signal or audio analysis anywhere in the paper.
findings.evidence: 3-0 verification against the extracted PDF text; the dataset paragraph is verbatim, and the record count is independently confirmed by the paper's own part-sampled tallies summing to exactly 42,447 (W 3060, D 15811, B 14329, V 913, H 7321, O 1013). Absence of audio analysis confirmed by grep of the full 6-page text: no signal/spectral/acoustic/feature analysis appears; 'audio' occurs only in related-work and bibliography. NOTE: the frequently cited URL ccrma.stanford.edu/~njb/research/influence.pdf now 404s — use the ISMIR archive or gewang.com mirror. Later WhoSampled-based network work (Figueiredo et al., arXiv 2410.15996, 'Surprising Patterns in Musical Influence Networks') uses larger scrapes without contradicting this description.

findings.claim: There is a concrete, reusable mechanism for propagating credit up a derivation chain toward the earliest ancestor — the operation a melodic-ancestry product needs — provided the graph already has directed edges. Bryan and Wang build an unweighted acyclic song-level graph (edges destination-to-source) and apply Katz centrality, I_K = (I - alpha*A)^-1 - I, where A^k counts sample chains of length k and alpha tunes how much indirect influence propagates; alpha=0 counts only direct sampling, alpha=1 weights direct and all indirect equally. PageRank was deliberately rejected because it 'down-weights influence created by a destination node that samples more than once, or ... artists with lengthy careers.' Empirically, for the 'Amen' break, credit moves from The Winstons (0.82 at alpha=0, absent from the top ten at alpha=1.0) toward Jester Hairston (the origin, appearing at 0.46 at alpha=1.0).
findings.evidence: Two 3-0 verifications; Table 2 reconstructed from PDF text and validated by strict monotonic non-increase within each alpha column. WhoSampled independently corroborates the chain (Winstons' 'Amen, Brother' samples The Impressions' 'We're a Winner'; 'Amen, Brother' is a cover of Hairston's 'Amen' from Lilies of the Field, 1963). Three honest deflations verifiers insisted on: (1) the intermediate 'to The Impressions' step is authorial prose, not visible in the alpha=0.2 column, and the Impressions entry at alpha=1.0 is 'We're a Winner,' not their 'Amen'; (2) alpha=1.0 does NOT put the earliest ancestor on top — Hairston lands at rank 10 of 10 in a three-way tie at 0.46, far below Change the Beat (1.0) and Funky Drummer (0.84); alpha accumulates transitive credit, it does not order ancestry; (3) the Amen case is a single illustrative anecdote with no ground truth and no accuracy number, and the paper does zero audio or melodic analysis. Also note alpha is not always constrained by the usual 1/alpha > largest-eigenvalue rule here, because on an acyclic song graph A^k vanishes beyond the maximum chain length.

findings.claim: No verified end-to-end system exists that takes an audio melody snippet and returns a directed provenance chain. Every verified component sits on one side of a gap: audio embeddings and symbolic aligners produce symmetric similarity with no direction; the phylogenetic toolchain produces trees but over manuscript witnesses of a single chant, needs symbolic monophonic input, and its rooting failed and needed manual override; the one multi-hop ancestry system runs on a hand-curated sampling database. In this verification corpus, directionality was in every case either supplied by human curation, encoded by construction, or determined by manual musicological judgment — never learned or inferred from the music itself.
findings.evidence: Synthesis across all verified findings; every verifier who touched a directionality question reached the same conclusion independently. Savage et al. 'estimates mutation/evolutionary rates and does NOT infer directionality or ancestry (who copied whom).' BMM-Det's pipeline is provably symmetric — 'No chronology, release date, or provenance signal enters anywhere in the pipeline, so the method structurally cannot assign direction.' MelodySim 'measures symmetric similarity only — it does not infer directionality/ancestry.' Bryan and Wang 'never claims to infer who-copied-whom from audio' and cite Collins on the difficulty of CONSTRUCTING influence networks, confirming inference is the hard part it sidesteps. Genome of Melody derives direction from tip-dating and Bayes-factor root selection, which failed on one of two datasets. Practical read for a builder: directionality in 2026 comes from release-date metadata plus a curated relationship graph, and the ML pipeline's job is candidate generation and localization, not adjudication.

findings.claim: SecondHandSongs' API does NOT verifiably expose the directed derivation graph it was claimed to: assertions that its Work resource carries reciprocal basedOn/derivedWorks link lists traversable into multi-hop ancestry chains, and that it designates a single canonical 'original' performance per work, were both rejected under adversarial verification.
findings.evidence: Two claims about the SHS Work endpoint were put to verification and failed: the basedOn/derivedWorks derivation-graph claim was refuted 0-3, and the canonical-original-performance claim was refuted 1-2. This is a negative result about what the verification could confirm from the cited documentation page, NOT positive proof that SHS lacks such fields — the underlying API may well model adaptations and originals in some form. Treat SHS as unverified-and-worth-checking-directly rather than as ruled out. Marked low confidence precisely because a refuted claim establishes little about the world.

result.caveats: COVERAGE IS THE BIGGEST CAVEAT. Only about eight primary sources survived into verified findings, and they cluster on cover-song embeddings, plagiarism detection, query-by-humming, folk-tune alignment, chant phylogenetics, and one sampling-network paper. Entire branches of the research question produced NO verified claims, and their absence here is not evidence of absence: (a) every commercial product named in the brief — Musical AI, Sureel, Pex, Audible Magic, ACRCloud (beyond its MIREX leaderboard rows), Rightsify/Sound Sample Detection, Matchtune, Deezer/Spotify internal work — and the melody-only limits of Shazam/SoundHound/Aha Music; (b) the knowledge-base layer other than WhoSampled: MusicBrainz work relationships, Discogs, Wikidata; (c) the symbolic-retrieval infrastructure named in the brief: Meertens Tune Collections / Dutch Song Database, Peachnote, Themefinder, Musipedia, SIMSSA (van Kranenburg surfaced only as corroborating context inside another finding); (d) the transcription and melody-extraction front-ends a real pipeline needs — basic-pitch, MT3, melodia, CREPE (CREPE appears only as a feature choice in one QbH table); (e) benchmark datasets DALI and MTG-Jamendo, and Da-TACOS/SHS100K/Covers80 beyond the numbers ByteCover reports; (f) the entire legal/musicological branch — forensic musicology expert-witness practice, substantial-similarity doctrine, public-domain and oral-tradition attribution, contrafacta, common melodic archetypes as a false-positive source. TIME SENSITIVITY: ByteCover's numbers are 2021 and superseded by ByteCover2/3 and CoverHunter; the QbH results are 2023 and should not be read as 2026 SOTA; Bryan and Wang is 2011 (the Katz mechanism does not expire, but nothing in it reflects modern retrieval practice). Only MelodySim (v2 Nov 2025), Genome of Melody (2025), and the SMP dataset (Sept 2025) are genuinely current. SOURCE ACCESS: the Royal Society article is paywalled and was verified via the authors' EcoEvoRxiv preprint plus an open-access PLOS ONE companion; Current Biology returns 403 to automated fetch and was verified via PubMed; the widely-cited ccrma.stanford.edu/~njb/research/influence.pdf URL is dead (use the ISMIR archive mirror). DOMAIN TRANSFER: the strongest evolutionary/alignment evidence comes from oral-transmission folk and chant repertoires, where variation is human-memory-mediated; extending those substitution matrices, indel rates and tree models to recording-mediated commercial pop borrowing — the actual Llorando se fue / Lambada / On the Floor case — is an untested extrapolation. GROUND TRUTH: reported accuracies on real infringement pairs rest on roughly 100 examples total across MCIC (116 cases, all labeled positive regardless of court outcome) and BMM-Det's 29 all-positive pairs, so precision estimates on real material are fragile. Finally, one refuted-claim finding is included for transparency; a refuted claim means verification could not confirm it from the cited page, not that the opposite is true.
openQuestions: Does any production system — commercial rights-clearance (Pex, Audible Magic, Musical AI, Sureel, ACRCloud) or platform-internal (Spotify, Deezer) — actually chain pairwise matches into a multi-hop derivation graph with inferred or metadata-derived directionality, or do they all stop at flagged pairwise pairs plus a human review queue? Nothing in this corpus touched their internals, and none publish comparable benchmark numbers on real infringement data.

Can release-date metadata plus a curated relationship graph (MusicBrainz work relationships, SecondHandSongs, WhoSampled, Discogs, Wikidata) supply directionality reliably enough to make the Katz-style credit propagation of Bryan and Wang work over MELODIC rather than sampling edges — and what does SecondHandSongs' Work API actually expose, given that two claims about its derivation fields were refuted rather than confirmed?

What is the real end-to-end accuracy of an audio-first pipeline (predominant-melody extraction or transcription, then symbolic n-gram/alignment retrieval, then candidate ranking) on cross-genre, cross-arrangement derivation cases? Every verified result is either audio-embedding-only or symbolic-only; the transcription front-end's error rate compounding into alignment scoring is entirely unmeasured here.

How should a system handle melodies with no single originator — public-domain folk material, oral-tradition variants, contrafacta, and common melodic archetypes that generate false positives? The Genome of Melody rooting failure and Savage et al.'s finding of zero highly-related cross-tradition pairs both suggest 'find the original' may be ill-posed for exactly the material where hooks most often come from, but no verified source in this corpus quantifies that false-positive rate or defines a usable abstention policy.

refuted.claim: The SecondHandSongs Work resource models an explicit, directed derivation graph between works — not just pairwise similarity — via two reciprocal link attributes, each typed as a list of work: `basedOn` (upstream ancestors) and `derivedWorks` (downstream descendants). This means SHS's API can be traversed recursively to reconstruct multi-hop melodic/compositional ancestry chains (e.g. Llorando se fue -> Lambada -> On the Floor), and directionality is asserted in the data rather than inferred.

The Work endpoint separates the abstract work from its recordings and designates a single canonical origin performance: it exposes `versions` (type: list of performance) for all versions of the work, and `original` (type: performance) for the original performance — so SHS encodes a curated ground-truth 'original' per work rather than leaving provenance ambiguous.

Reconstructing an actual ancestral MELODY (as opposed to a tree of sources) is only at pilot stage: ancestral state reconstruction has been shown 'possible' in a prior pilot but is not part of this study, and the authors explicitly deny that a single original melody exists to be recovered — a direct caveat for any 'find the original source' product built on folk/traditional material.
